label: Future of developer work → 2031
summary: Plain-language map of a multi-day AI research investigation. Every claim links to its source notes and URLs.

children.label: How to prepare (and risks)
children.summary: Aim to deliver systems that others accept and keep using, not just write code. This is a hypothesis to test with small experiments, not a promise of jobs in 2031.
headlines: Core bet: own accepted outcomes. Understand a real system, use AI and native tools well, measure failures and cost, and maintain what others rely on.
Cloud vendors already bundle evals, agents and incident tools, and AI research-engineering results are strong. Neither custom integration nor research is automatically safe.
Useful skills, paid roles, high pay and a startup moat are four separate things. More output with fewer people is a realistic 2031 outcome.
Start with one 30-day experiment against a strong native baseline. Stop if the native tool wins or no independent check of the right answer exists.
Leadership comes from a real project accepting your work, you maintaining it through change, then being trusted with responsibility. No dates or titles are promised.

children.label: Core thesis
children.summary: Prepare to own outcomes that others accept and maintain, using AI and native tools sensibly.

children.label: Own accepted outcomes
children.summary: Understand the system, pick AI vs ready-made tools, integrate, measure failures and cost, maintain what others depend on. A hypothesis to test, not a forecast.

children.label: Code alone is a weaker identity
children.summary: Inference: producing plausible code matters less. Choosing the problem, directing automation and maintaining accepted work matters more. AI can automate those too.

children.label: Ordinary backend work stays valid
children.summary: Backend, data and platform engineering remains a fine path. There is no protected human niche and no guaranteed scarce job here.

children.label: Pick one depth, not five courses
children.summary: Choose one route and compare it to a competent ready-made tool. If the native tool solves it, drop the extra custom work.

children.label: Keep four outcomes separate
children.summary: Useful skill, number of paid roles, high wages and a defensible startup are different. Evidence for one is not evidence for the others.

children.label: 2031 scenarios
children.summary: Three possible worlds, not predictions. Different sectors can sit in different worlds at once.

children.label: Slower, uneven adoption
children.summary: Procurement, data access and acceptance slow deployment. Risk: years spent on a frontier specialty nobody can adopt. Response: improve an accessible workflow.

children.label: Platforms absorb the work
children.summary: Big platforms and employers automate the whole loop; a smaller expert group supervises more. Risk: becoming good at a feature vendors bundle.

children.label: Cheap autonomy for everyone
children.summary: Strong tools are widely usable and many people build products. Risk: your output is not scarce; distribution, not code, limits income.

children.label: More output, fewer people
children.summary: Made-up example: 100 jobs at 20 hours becomes 300 jobs at 2 hours; total human hours fall from 2,200 to 650. Accountability alone does not guarantee more seats.

children.label: Counter-arguments
children.summary: Evidence that weakened early recommendations, and evidence pushing back the other way.

children.label: Vendors already bundle evals and agents
children.summary: Cloud platforms ship managed agents, policy, evaluation and incident tools. Demand can rise while human effort per deployment falls.

children.label: AWS AgentCore release notes
children.summary: Documents managed execution, policy and identity, online and batch evaluation, custom evaluators and A/B tests. Product availability is shown; real adoption is not.

children.label: AWS DevOps Agent generally available
children.summary: Targets incident investigation and SRE work, announced 31 March 2026. Vendor claim, not independent proof it replaces engineers.

children.label: Palantir platform already has agents
children.summary: Its platform includes workflow, agent and evaluation tools while it also hires customer-facing engineers. Weakens 'any custom integration layer will be valuable'.

children.label: Research is not safe from automation
children.summary: Moving into research does not escape AI. Several results show agents doing research-engineering tasks well, within narrow limits.

children.label: RE-Bench kernel beat all humans
children.summary: An AI kernel solution beat all nine human attempts on one task. But: 7 selected tasks, 2024 models, 71 attempts by 61 people; not a whole research job.

children.label: Epoch automated its own chart task
children.summary: A chart-restyling task was removed after AI handled it. Eleven selected tasks, one run per model; partial scores are not jobs automated.

children.label: Entry-level ladder is narrowing
children.summary: At one fast-growing lab, junior technical hires fell from 27% to 9% of hires while headcount grew. Exceptional employer, observational data.

children.label: AI coding gains cut both ways
children.summary: Company experiments (mostly 2022-24) show developer gains; a small study of experienced maintainers found a slowdown. Different people and tools; neither measures 5-year jobs.

children.label: No clear job losses yet
children.summary: A survey of about 6,000 executives found roughly 9 in 10 saw no past employment effect; a BIS study found 4% productivity gain, no job loss. Expectations, not 2031.

children.label: Skill shortages are not funded jobs
children.summary: ISC2 survey of 16,029 people: 33% say teams cannot be staffed, 29% cannot afford needed skills. Need does not mean vacancies.

children.label: Plan may just echo your interests
children.summary: Recommending the robotics-AI-software overlap because it matches your history is a fit guess. Compare real alternatives: systems depth, enterprise domain, research, sales.

children.label: Career progression ladder
children.summary: Five proposed milestones from learner to trusted owner. Milestones, not promised dates, titles or pay.

children.label: 1. Prove basics on one fresh test
children.summary: Show prerequisites on one independent test case before widening scope. Skip anything you already know. Stop if no independent check exists.

children.label: 2. Reproduce a known result
children.summary: Re-create a published or native-tool result within its stated versions, rights and resources. A reproduced result is a checkpoint, not novelty.

children.label: 3. Explain a gap, prepare a contribution
children.summary: Explain a leftover discrepancy using untouched cases and total effort, then prepare a change that fits a real project's review rules.

children.label: 4. Get accepted, then maintain it
children.summary: After a real project accepts your work, keep it working through changes, triage regressions and document decisions so others can continue.

children.label: 5. Take entrusted responsibility
children.summary: Seek accountability for an outcome, budget, reliability boundary or small team only when a real receiver entrusts it. Merged code, pay and leadership are separate.

children.label: What leadership frameworks reward
children.summary: Public frameworks reward sustained scope, reviews, handoffs and trusted decisions, not titles or commit counts.

children.label: Dropbox: next-level impact over time
children.summary: Promotion needs demonstrated next-level impact sustained over time, not promise. Includes keeping systems maintainable by others. Internal framework, not a portable title.

children.label: NumPy steering council entry
children.summary: Needs substantial contributions for at least a year, plus nomination and consensus. Review, docs and helping others count, not just commits.

children.label: No calendar promises a title
children.summary: No defensible timeline gives a title, reputation or wage by 2031. Public repo, accepted patch, paid work and entrusted ownership are different wins.

children.label: Routes into open-source and funded work
children.summary: Real routes exist, but nearly all need a receiving project, open dates and eligibility. Check the gate before preparing.

children.label: Start with a requested test
children.summary: Most credible entry: a regression test or benchmark fix a maintainer has asked for. Example: PyVRP maintainers asked about short CI benchmarks. No pay or acceptance guaranteed.

children.label: Paid maintenance needs a project
children.summary: Funding buys scoped work, services or milestones, not a salary. Sovereign Tech Fund needs work over 50,000 euros; LFX 2026 window closed 18 August.

children.label: Research routes hinge on eligibility
children.summary: Funded research entry exists in different forms. Each has a first gate: degree, work rights, location or enrolment. None is shown best for you.

children.label: Anthropic Fellows
children.summary: Four-month mentored research stipend. No PhD or publications required, but needs US, UK or Canada work authorization and offers no visa sponsorship.

children.label: STFC graduate programme
children.summary: Two-year permanent-contract development programme with computing pathways; 2027 opening announced. Role, site and sponsorship unverified.

children.label: Bristol AI doctoral programme
children.summary: Funded four-year PhD for 2027, applications open; needs coding evidence and a case study. Offer and funding are separate decisions.

children.label: 'AI engineer' jobs differ widely
children.summary: One saved ad stresses production software and GPU infrastructure; another stresses research track record. Indexed ads, not verified vacancies.

children.label: Starter experiments
children.summary: Five alternative 30/90-day experiments. Pick one; each stops if the native tool wins or no independent truth exists.

children.label: Rule for every experiment
children.summary: First check prerequisites and access. Then test one baseline against an independent answer key. Success: a result a stranger could verify.

children.label: Workflow state and recovery
children.summary: 30 days: trace request to simulated effect, testing duplicates, stale inputs, lost acknowledgements against an independent ledger. 90 days: schema changes, recovery, full-cost comparison. Stop if native workflow suffices.

children.label: Evaluation and scorer tooling
children.summary: 30 days: use a mature harness; test 25-50 deliberate scorer cases, including wrong answers accepted. 90 days: reproduce one result or explain a discrepancy. Stop if harness covers it.

children.label: As-of data platform
children.summary: 30 days: study one permitted dataset's units, publication times and revisions; plain SQL is the baseline. 90 days: analyst task only if real data and a reviewer exist. Stop otherwise.

children.label: Health or lab software (synthetic)
children.summary: 30 days: write a lab-runner state contract, or reconcile synthetic non-clinical health records. 90 days: re-run across interruptions and version changes. Stop without independent truth; simulation is not lab validity.

children.label: AI serving memory ledger
children.summary: First 4-6 hours: hand-count weights vs KV cache memory. Then 32-48 hours comparing one native setup. Continue only for a reproducible gap; native win stops. Hour totals still unsettled.

children.label: Foundations that transfer
children.summary: Six skills reused across routes. Show them with a real artifact; stronger AI may do some of them too.

children.label: Read and debug unfamiliar code
children.summary: Explain the dataflow, predict a broken rule, find evidence for the cause, fix it, then handle a new variant.

children.label: Identity, state, time, provenance
children.summary: Trace any output to its source and version. Handle duplicates, late revisions, unknown values and units.

children.label: Independent correctness checks
children.summary: Audit both the tool and the answer key. Find cases where wrong answers pass and right answers fail.

children.label: Measurement and honest comparison
children.summary: Match conditions, keep failed attempts and total effort, explain uncertainty. Product, ML and science decisions all need this.

children.label: Authority, handoff, collaboration
children.summary: Name the real owner and error consequences, keep permissions aligned with effects, and hand the system over so others can run it.

children.label: New fields add real depth
children.summary: Switching fields reuses habits but adds depth: health data adds FHIR identity and clinical meaning; GPU work adds C++ and numerics. Job ads still set degree and location filters.

children.label: AI help and real learning
children.summary: Evidence on whether AI-assisted learners keep skills is thin and mixed; measure unaided ability separately.

children.label: Delayed design task study
children.summary: Small student study: median delayed score 32.67% AI vs 51.83% control, not statistically significant. Unclear harm, not proof of none.

children.label: Predict before you ask AI
children.summary: Predict or explain unaided first, then use AI. A week later, try a new task without help. Success: you can repair it alone. Stop if you cannot.

children.label: Jobs & hiring evidence
children.summary: Hiring of young workers in AI-exposed jobs looks weak, but nobody has proven AI is the cause, and no study shows mass developer job loss. Experienced, production-owning engineers still look safest.
headlines: Young (22-25) workers in AI-exposed jobs are 19% below peers in US payroll data, mostly through less hiring, but the authors say this is descriptive, not proof AI caused it.
Studies disagree on AI's causal effect: Danish and US macro data show little aggregate damage, while one Danish firm study finds adopters hired less than their trend.
Employers still ask for ordinary strong backend, data and testing skills plus AI integration; eligibility (country, visas, clearance) often blocks more than skills do.

children.label: Entry-level squeeze
children.summary: Several independent datasets show weaker hiring of young workers in AI-exposed work. Others show no clear AI footprint overall.

children.label: US payroll: 22-25s are 19% below peers
children.summary: Stanford/ADP payroll data to June 2026: young workers in AI-exposed jobs trail comparison peers by 19%, via less hiring. Older workers show no gap. Authors call it descriptive, not causal.

children.label: It is a relative gap, not 19% fired
children.summary: The 19% compares exposed jobs with less-exposed peers. It shrinks with education controls, has some pretrend differences, and the sample only includes firms that survived the whole period.

children.label: Census data also shows young-worker weakness
children.summary: An independent Census study (administrative records) confirms weak young-worker employment and hiring in highly exposed industries. It does not prove AI caused a 12% job loss.

children.label: Ads: entry share fell 29% to 10%
children.summary: Indeed: in the most AI-exposed salaried US ads, entry-level share fell 29% to 10% while senior rose 22% to 47%. Sample skews senior; ads are not hires.

children.label: US macro data shows no clear AI footprint
children.summary: Yale Budget Lab (Oct 2026): job mix and unemployment are not changing in line with AI. But its data is too thin to rule out narrow entry-level damage.

children.label: Danish worker survey: no earnings or hours hit
children.summary: 25k Danish workers linked to payroll records through 2024: chatbot-adopting firms did not drive early-career declines, and average earnings effects are ruled out above 2%. Window is older and Danish.

children.label: Does AI actually cause it?
children.summary: No study cleanly proves AI is the cause. Results flip depending on country, period, and whether you measure adoption or exposure.

children.label: Danish firms that adopted AI hired less
children.summary: Danmarks Nationalbank: firms adopting AI in 2023 had 11% lower employment growth than non-adopters by late 2025, mostly small firms cutting recruitment. Employment still grew overall.

children.label: Authors say it is descriptive, not causal
children.summary: The result compares firms to their own pre-AI trend. A slowdown, restructuring or demand shock at adopting firms could look identical.

children.label: Europe-wide survey points the other way
children.summary: ECB analysis of about 5,300 euro-area firms: heavy AI users were about 4 percentage points more likely to add workers. Profitable firms may just adopt more.

children.label: Most executives report no effect yet
children.summary: NBER survey of nearly 6,000 executives (US/UK/Germany/Australia): about nine in ten see no employment or productivity effect so far. Executives expect -0.7% jobs, employees +0.5%.

children.label: Faster work does not equal fewer jobs
children.summary: If each unit takes 20% fewer human hours, total hours can fall, stay flat or rise depending on how much more output gets funded. Speed gains alone cannot predict headcount.

children.label: Adoption numbers are not automation numbers
children.summary: US estimates range from 18% of firms to 78% of employment-weighted firms using AI, depending on definition. None means that share of work is automated.

children.label: Official forecasts and surveys
children.summary: Government and institutional projections say developer demand keeps growing in the US, while narrow coding-only roles shrink.

children.label: US developers: +10% growth to 2035
children.summary: BLS (Aug 2026): software developers, QA and testers go from 1,905,400 to 2,090,800 jobs, with 106,100 openings a year. Developer median pay $135,980. US only, not entry-level odds.

children.label: Pure programmers: -7% projected
children.summary: BLS projects the narrower programmer occupation falling from 110,800 to 102,700, blaming automation of repetitive coding. Whole-system developers are projected to grow instead.

children.label: Neighbouring roles grow faster
children.summary: BLS: data scientists +35%, information-security analysts +21%. High percentages come from smaller bases; general software still has far more openings.

children.label: Global surveys: churn, not collapse
children.summary: WEF employers expect 170m jobs created and 92m displaced by 2030, with developers among fastest growing. ILO says 25% of global jobs are exposed. Both are expectations, not measured losses.

children.label: India hiring
children.summary: India's tech export base is still growing, but big services firms show flat or falling headcount while AI revenue rises. Aggregates say little about one developer's odds.

children.label: Software exports $221.4bn, up 8.2%
children.summary: RBI FY2025-26: grossed-up exports $221.4bn. US takes 54.1%, Europe 31.8% (UK 15.4%). Covers IT services, BPO and engineering, not developer employment.

children.label: Big services firms: AI up, headcount flat
children.summary: Infosys reports AI at 8.2% of revenue yet closing staff fell 532 in the quarter. Wipro fell 6,716 in a quarter. HCLTech added 6,450 net, 6,136 of them freshers.

children.label: Headcount changes are not layoff counts
children.summary: Closing staff mixes hires, exits, acquisitions, transfers and contractors. A drop does not show AI caused job cuts, and a rise does not show AI created jobs.

children.label: Contracts are leaving the hourly model
children.summary: Wipro already books 52.4% of revenue as fixed-price. If AI cuts hours per task, firms that bill by the hour lose revenue while fixed-price firms keep margin.

children.label: GCCs: 2,117 centres, 2.36m staff
children.summary: Zinnov-Nasscom counts 2,117 captive centres with 2.36m workforce. Vendors also build and run these centres, so a GCC can move jobs between employers without creating any.

children.label: AI skills rising in Indian job ads
children.summary: World Bank ads: AI-related share went 2.89% (Jan 2023) to 6.51% (Mar 2025); AI-skill ads advertised about 28% higher pay. Ads skew urban white-collar; pay is advertised only.

children.label: Indian firms use AI less than US firms
children.summary: World Bank 2026 survey of 1,355 Indian establishments: 23.36% use any AI versus 42.68% in the US. 'Any AI' includes basic chatbots, so it is a loose measure.

children.label: UK and remote eligibility
children.summary: UK and global-remote demand exists, but residence, visa and clearance rules often decide who can apply, regardless of skill.

children.label: UK survey: 97% report an AI skills gap
children.summary: UK government survey: 97% of 119 AI-active firms report some skills gap. Only 3% of invited organisations replied, and 111 of 119 were small firms. Not a national shortage estimate.

children.label: UK entry routes: graduates and career-changers
children.summary: In the same survey, 60% of organisations hired career starters and 74% hired from non-AI roles. Apprenticeships were used by 19% of organisations but only 3% of the AI workforce.

children.label: Remote does not mean worldwide
children.summary: GitLab's agent-backend role is open to Canada, Poland and UK, not India. Atlassian's responsible-AI role is remote only within India. A UK security-cleared role needs five years' UK residence.

children.label: What employers actually ask for
children.summary: Real postings want solid backend, data and testing fundamentals, with AI work layered on top. Frontier-lab roles and pay are rare outliers.

children.label: Sample of 15 roles at 11 employers
children.summary: Hand-picked India/UK roles: backend, data engineering, DevOps, test automation, applied AI, robotics. Only four showed a posting date and four showed pay. Not a demand estimate.

children.label: Agent roles rest on ordinary backend skills
children.summary: GitLab's agent role wants APIs, async jobs, tests, evaluations and on-call, with no PhD listed. Its India backend role asks candidates to validate AI-generated code.

children.label: Frontier-lab forward-deployed engineer
children.summary: Anthropic London: production agents, evaluations, customer discovery, 25-50% travel, GBP 225k-255k. The ad says both 4+ and 8+ years. An outlier comparator, not a normal pay benchmark.

children.label: Robotics roles need depth, not just ROS
children.summary: Aeva's Bangalore perception role wants 3+ years, an MS/PhD, C++, geometry and sensor fusion; ROS is only nice-to-have. A ROS2 course alone does not cover it.

children.label: Interview AI rules differ by company and round
children.summary: Six employers differ: some rounds expect AI use (Canva, Datadog's designated rounds), most default to none. Anthropic allowed AI only in one named take-home. Always check the specific stage.

children.label: Credentials and bootcamps
children.summary: Courses can raise measured skill, but job and pay gains are small, uneven or unproven. Diagnose your actual bottleneck before buying one.

children.label: Easy-to-share credentials: +1 point new jobs
children.summary: Randomised test of a credential-sharing nudge: new job reports rose about 1.0 percentage point at one month. The 4-month effect is not clearly different from zero.

children.label: Coding bootcamp RCT: skills up, jobs mixed
children.summary: World Bank trial with 803 women in Argentina and Colombia: test scores rose and coding employment +6.7 points, but overall employment fell 7.2 points and no clear earnings gain.

children.label: 10-year US training study: IT provider faded
children.summary: MDRC randomised 2,564 adults. The IT provider's earnings gain was +$1,971 and not significant at year 10; one non-IT provider showed +$8,580. Low-income adults, not developers.

children.label: No study prices a course for you
children.summary: None of this estimates the return to buying a particular course for an employed AI engineer. A fix must match the gap: skill, proof of skill, or access.

children.label: Freelancing
children.summary: The best paid-market study covers writers, not developers, and found fewer jobs and lower pay after ChatGPT. Developer freelance evidence is missing.

children.label: Writers: jobs and pay fell after ChatGPT
children.summary: Platform data on 79,322 freelancers: writing-exposed freelancers saw a 1.2 point drop in landing any job and lower pay versus other occupations after ChatGPT's release.

children.label: No developer-specific freelance data
children.summary: The study gives no estimate of developer earnings or 2031 demand. Rival explanations like a post-COVID demand unwind are not ruled out.

children.label: Jobs and skills to build toward
children.summary: The evidence favours roles that own a system in production, with evaluation, security and customer ownership, over roles that only turn tickets into code.

children.label: Backend/data engineer who owns recovery
children.summary: Production services, databases, migrations and debugging appear across ordinary employers. Still exposed to AI-assisted coding, so the edge is reliable independent ownership.

children.label: Applied AI engineer on a solid backend
children.summary: Models inside real workflows with a plain baseline, held-out tests and recovery. Capgemini's AI data role explicitly does not require all AI experience up front.

children.label: Evaluation and security specialist
children.summary: Atlassian's senior responsible-AI role shows software, ML and security combined. It needs 7+ years, so treat it as a later destination, not a first job.

children.label: Production reliability and testing
children.summary: Tests, observability, failure injection, incident write-ups and design trade-offs travel across tools and model generations better than any one framework.

children.label: Statistics and evaluation design
children.summary: Held-out data, leakage, baselines and calibrating graders are needed to prove an AI feature works. A slick demo with no denominator is not evidence.

children.label: Concrete next steps
children.summary: Cheap ways to test where you stand and which role family fits, each with a clear sign it is working or should stop.

children.label: 30 days: run four diagnostic exercises
children.summary: Build a failure-prone integration service, a holdout model comparison, an incident postmortem and a customer-interview-to-test. Log what AI got wrong. Working: you can verify answers unaided. Stop: gaps stay unfixed.

children.label: 30 days: filter roles by eligibility first
children.summary: List 10 roles. Cross out those blocked by country, visa, clearance or hard degree filters before comparing skills. Working: 3-4 reachable role families remain. Stop: none remain, so widen geography.

children.label: 90 days: add AI beside a baseline
children.summary: Put a model beside a manual or rule-based baseline. Measure errors, cost, latency, recovery on held-out cases. Working: it beats baseline. Stop if a native tool already does it.

children.label: Ongoing: watch hiring rates, not layoffs
children.summary: Track hiring and employment by age and tenure, entry share in ads, and funded output at your own employer. Reduced hiring hurts opportunity before headcount falls. Revise if hiring recovers.

children.label: GitLab: contributions are asked for
children.summary: Its India backend application form asks for open-source project links, so a maintained contribution is inspectable proof. Its roles also stress validating AI-generated code.

children.label: Monzo: learns-the-stack, no-degree policy
children.summary: UK bank says it supports learning its stack rather than requiring every listed technology, and has a stated no-degree policy for engineering. Relocation and sponsorship possible; pay GBP 85k-110k base.

children.label: Risk: platforms absorb the specialist loop
children.summary: If native tools or agents handle requirements, integration, evaluation and incident response cheaply, one small team covers more output and the specialist niche shrinks.

children.label: Software & AI engineering
children.summary: AI agents are getting much better at long, checkable software tasks, but evidence that they raise real-world output or replace engineers is mixed. Work with cheap, trustworthy checking automates first; owning the checking loop looks most durable.
headlines: Agents can now do long, well-specified coding tasks, but the headline numbers are fragile: bad graders, cheating attempts and wide error bars distort them.
Real-world productivity evidence conflicts: one study found 19% slowdown, another 26% more pull requests, and METR's 2026 follow-up was inconclusive.
Tasks with a cheap, trustworthy way to check the answer (ports, migrations, clear specs) automate first; building and auditing the checks is the safest skill to own.
Entry paths exist (eval, inference/serving, GPU/compiler, migrations), but most sampled employer roles want 5+ years, so build a public, checkable artifact first.

children.label: How capable are coding agents now?
children.summary: Task length agents can finish is rising fast, but every measurement has known holes.

children.label: Task horizon doubling every ~131 days
children.summary: METR: the task length (human time) that models finish half the time doubled every 131 days since 2023, versus about seven months on the longer history.

children.label: Only 5 long tasks had real human timings
children.summary: Of 31 tasks of 8+ hours, just five had measured human baselines; the rest are estimates. Fits change a lot with the period chosen.

children.label: A 50% success horizon is not reliable work
children.summary: Half-the-time success on a task length is not dependable unattended work. No current 95% reliability horizon was found; METR's chart stopped updating in September 2026.

children.label: Cheating attempts can swing results 25x
children.summary: METR on GPT-5.6 Sol: counting cheats as failures gives about 11.3 hours; as successes, over 270; dropping them, about 71. METR says none is a robust measure.

children.label: Exact reimplementation of programs works
children.summary: MirrorCode: agents rebuild command-line programs from documentation plus a runnable reference, with hidden tests. The Pkl program stayed unsolved after extensive debugging.

children.label: FrontierSWE v2: 34 hard tasks, 20 hours each
children.summary: Top scores: GPT-6 Astra 65.5%, Claude Opus 5.5 62.3%. These are partial-credit averages, not share of jobs or tasks fully solved. One run cost about $97.

children.label: Benchmarks can be wrong both ways
children.summary: OpenAI found at least 59.4% of 138 audited SWE-bench Verified problems had tests rejecting correct fixes. Epoch flagged 23 of 113 DeepSWE tasks as defective.

children.label: Messy office work: about 65% rubric score
children.summary: Epoch's 11 real tasks: top models score 65% against employee standards. That is partial credit, not 65% of jobs automated. Epoch automated one easy task internally.

children.label: Does AI actually make developers faster?
children.summary: Studies disagree because they measure different things in different settings.

children.label: Copilot field trials: 26% more pull requests
children.summary: Three company experiments (4,867 developers): +26.08% PRs, but this is a weighted estimate for adopters. Early-window gains were small and not significant (about +4.7%).

children.label: Experienced devs were 19% slower (2025)
children.summary: METR: 16 veterans, 246 issues in familiar repos took 19% longer with AI (CI +2% to +39%). Early-2025 tools, narrow setting.

children.label: 2026 follow-up was inconclusive
children.summary: Newer METR study: -18% and -4% time, both intervals include no effect. Developers refused no-AI tasks, so METR calls the signal unreliable.

children.label: Anthropic: junior technical hires 27% to 9%
children.summary: Share of junior technical hires fell while technical headcount still grew. A single fast-growing company, observational data; not a forecast for all employers.

children.label: Support agents resolved 15% more per hour
children.summary: Study of 5,172 support agents (2019-2021, not randomized): +15.2% resolutions per hour, biggest gains for novices, small quality dips for top performers.

children.label: Klarna: 80% of chats, but no clean cause
children.summary: Company says AI handles 80% of chats; employees fell by 591. Support cost went $203M to $207M. Filings do not show AI caused the job cuts.

children.label: AI help can cost you learning
children.summary: RCT of 52 coders: AI-assisted group scored 4.15 points lower (of 27) on an unaided quiz; finishing time was not significantly faster. Small, one-library test.

children.label: What makes work easier or harder to automate?
children.summary: Cheap, trustworthy checking looks like the deciding factor, not just task length.

children.label: Work with a cheap correctness check goes first
children.summary: A long port with a runnable reference may automate before a short ambiguous customer decision. This is the research's own hypothesis, not a proven law.

children.label: Agents can still ace the grader and fail
children.summary: A hardcoded expected path can reject correct work, and a final-state check can accept a forbidden action. Verifiers need auditing too.

children.label: Repeat success is much lower than one-shot
children.summary: tau-bench 2024: 61.2% single-run retail success but under 25% when all eight runs must succeed. Old models, but the measuring lesson holds.

children.label: Code written by agents may age worse
children.summary: CodeThread: later agent fixes failed more often on agent-written code (12 worse, 3 better, 1 tied in the main table, up to 13 points). Agent-only test, no human maintainers.

children.label: Evolving-codebase tests are still immature
children.summary: SWE-EVO uses 48 release-to-release upgrades in seven Python repos. It tests single upgrades, not months of continuous maintenance. SlopCodeBench is similar.

children.label: Agent memory is tested; permission is not
children.summary: MemoryArena (701 task groups) tests carrying info between sessions. It does not test deleting or correcting memory, or whether the agent is allowed to act.

children.label: Database tuning by LLM: real gains, narrow proof
children.summary: GenRewrite (2024) sped up some TPC-DS queries, but on one benchmark, with failures scored as no speedup and equivalence only partly checked.

children.label: Proof-writing is automating; meaning-checking is not
children.summary: AlphaVerus and Verus-SpecGym (77.8% pass@1) show AI writes code plus proofs. Whether the statement matches the real requirement still needs independent checks.

children.label: Platforms keep absorbing the easy layer
children.summary: AWS DMS already offers optional AI schema conversion; vLLM and Inspect already cover many 'missing' features. Custom tools must beat native ones at lower total cost.

children.label: Roles that exist
children.summary: Sampled public job pages show where the work is; most want years of experience.

children.label: Evaluation / AI reliability engineer
children.summary: Designs tasks, scorers and checks; finds failures benchmarks miss. Mistral's eval-platform role wants 4+ years and a Master's or equivalent; Cohere's wants a senior evaluation record.

children.label: Inference / serving engineer
children.summary: Make models serve more requests at a latency target per GPU. Needs memory, scheduling and profiling skills; senior roles expect multi-node experience.

children.label: ML research engineer
children.summary: Reproduce and extend research with honest negative results. Generic API wiring does not count; research-scientist titles may need a doctorate.

children.label: Forward-deployed / applied AI engineer
children.summary: Integrate AI into messy customer workflows and prove accepted outcomes with measured human effort and cost. One narrow end-to-end system is a credible entry proof.

children.label: GPU kernel / compiler engineer
children.summary: Numerical correctness and speed on accelerators. Sampled roles: Arm runtime role accepts open-source C++ evidence; NVIDIA compiler role wants 8+ years.

children.label: Migration and data-correctness owner
children.summary: Own what the target data must match and how failed runs resume. AI drafts the SQL; a well-specified migration test gets more valuable, not less.

children.label: Formal verification engineer
children.summary: Rare and experience-heavy: Arm's role wants 5+ years in chip verification. Could grow if AI code spreads, or be automated in-house; the evidence cannot say.

children.label: Skills worth learning
children.summary: Skills that let you check, measure and diagnose, not just prompt.

children.label: Write tests that can fail themselves
children.summary: Build graders, hidden variants and fault injection; measure false accepts and false rejects. Report all attempts, not only successes.

children.label: Systems profiling: memory, caches, latency
children.summary: Explain a bottleneck before changing code; compare at matched quality, latency and cost. Needed for serving, compilers and databases.

children.label: Stats for evals: error bars, repeats
children.summary: Clean 100 test cases still allows roughly a 3% real failure rate. Learn confidence intervals, clustering and repeated-trial metrics.

children.label: Keep unaided coding and debugging sharp
children.summary: Test yourself without the assistant. The RCT shows finished output can hide weak understanding.

children.label: What to do next
children.summary: Small, checkable projects with a stop rule beat open-ended courses.

children.label: 30 days: build a scorer that tests itself
children.summary: Make 12 small tasks with hidden variants plus planted bad solutions; inject grader faults. Worked if every planted fault is caught; stop if grader and candidate share a bug.

children.label: 90 days: compare cheap proxy to accepted outcome
children.summary: Expand to 24-40 held-out tasks with a later change request. Worked if test-pass rate and strict acceptance diverge measurably; stop if savings vanish after review.

children.label: 30 days: profile one serving workload
children.summary: Pick one supported model, fixed request trace; measure time-to-first-token, p95/p99 latency and quality; explain a bottleneck. Worked if a fix beats baseline at matched budget.

children.label: Report one reproducible benchmark defect
children.summary: Find a score that changes under a specific flaw; write a minimal reproduction and corrected test. Worked if maintainers confirm it; stop if a simpler explanation fits.

children.label: Teams to learn from or contribute to
children.summary: Open evaluation and serving projects accept public contributions; none promises a job.

children.label: METR and Epoch AI
children.summary: Run the time-horizon and automation benchmarks. Learn how task design, cost curves and audits work; contribute through public repositories.

children.label: vLLM, SGLang and Inspect AI
children.summary: Open serving and evaluation code with public issues. Good places for a small regression test or measurement fix.

children.label: Triton, MLX and llama.cpp
children.summary: Kernel and on-device runtime communities; contributions require a minimal regression test and maintainer review.

children.label: Debezium and PostgreSQL communities
children.summary: Public routes into data-migration correctness; start with a minimized snapshot or replication test case.

children.label: AI hardware, power & geopolitics
children.summary: AI runs on a chain of physical things: chips, memory, fabs, packaging, networks, power. Chips are being shipped, but the real limits are often power and workload fit. Developers can help in specific software corners; none is guaranteed.
headlines: AI needs a long physical chain (chips, HBM memory, fabs, packaging, networking, power); being announced is not the same as being built, qualified and powered.
Which part limits you depends on the workload, and memory shortage is not a safe permanent career bet; both chip makers and software can relieve it.
Reachable developer work is real but narrow: serving/memory software, accelerator compilers, open EDA, SSD firmware tooling, energy and grid data. Native tools and AI already automate much of it.
Export controls and country dependence are layered and change often; the research could not confirm full current law or your personal eligibility.

children.label: What AI physically depends on
children.summary: The chain from chip design to a powered, cooled building. Each step has different units, so numbers from one step cannot be reused for another.

children.label: Accelerators: chip, module, rack differ
children.summary: NVIDIA, AMD, Google TPU and AWS Trainium sell different units (chip, module, 72-GPU rack). Peak specs are not real application speed.

children.label: Memory is six different things
children.summary: SRAM, DDR, HBM, GDDR, LPDDR and NAND have different roles. HBM is stacked memory next to the chip, not a bigger DIMM.

children.label: HBM4 is shipping, with vendor caveats
children.summary: Samsung reports commercial HBM4: up to 3.3 TB/s per stack, 24-36 GB. 'Stable yield' is stated without numbers. SK hynix mass-ships HBM4; HBM4E is samples.

children.label: HBM eats more fab space per bit
children.summary: Micron's filing says HBM uses more wafers and cleanroom per bit than normal DRAM. Weaker HBM demand could free up conventional DRAM supply.

children.label: Fabs and tools: many countries, one chain
children.summary: Advanced chips need qualified fabs plus an international equipment chain. TSMC reports real production; ASML makes tools across four countries. A fab announcement is not volume output.

children.label: Packaging and materials need qualification
children.summary: Wafers, interposers, substrates and finished packages are different units. TSMC's material table also counters a blanket-shortage story. Current packaging yield data was not found.

children.label: Networking and storage: fast parts, unclear gains
children.summary: Broadcom ships a 102.4 Tbps switch chip; NVIDIA's GB300 rack links 72 GPUs. Faster links or SSDs still do not guarantee more useful AI work without checking the workload.

children.label: Optical networking is not optical computing
children.summary: Optical links are in production. Computing with light is still early: lab papers and small deployments, with no proven edge over digital chips.

children.label: What is actually bottlenecked
children.summary: The limit moves: compute, memory, network, storage or power, depending on the job. Power and grid connection are the most repeated constraint.

children.label: Bottleneck depends on the workload
children.summary: Training, prefill, decode and retrieval each hit a different limit. Measure accepted outputs under deadlines, not peak arithmetic or tokens per second.

children.label: Data centre power demand doubles by 2030
children.summary: IEA estimates data centres used 485 TWh in 2025 and projects about 950 TWh in 2030, around 3% of world electricity. It is a scenario, not a certainty.

children.label: Grid connection queues are huge
children.summary: IEA counts 1,700 GW of renewable projects and 600 GW of batteries waiting for grid connection in 2025. Operators cite skills, data and trust as barriers to using AI.

children.label: Announced is not energized
children.summary: Announced megawatts, energy contracts and delivered chips are not a powered, cooled, accepted site. Utilities stage commissioning, and power equipment is itself short.

children.label: Memory shortage is not a safe forever bet
children.summary: Supplier expansion and software efficiency can each ease the squeeze or move it elsewhere. Revenue growth is not bit capacity. No 2031 shortage forecast is supported.

children.label: Who controls it: geopolitics and India
children.summary: Each stage sits in different countries, and export rules are layered. The research read part of the law and says so.

children.label: Stages are spread across countries
children.summary: OECD maps US design and EDA, Taiwan foundry and packaging, Korea memory, Japan wafers and tools, Netherlands EUV. Headquarters is not where chips are made.

children.label: 87% of fab capacity is in five places
children.summary: OECD puts 87% of in-production wafer capacity (Sept 2025) in China, Taiwan, Korea, Japan and the US. It counts wafer starts, not usable AI chips.

children.label: US export controls are layered
children.summary: A January 2026 rule allows case-by-case review for some chip exports to China below set performance limits. May 2026 guidance eased new AI Diffusion rules but older parent-company limits remain.

children.label: Rules cover HBM, EDA software and US persons
children.summary: A Dec 2024 rule sets HBM bandwidth-density limits, some chip-design (EDA) software controls, and foreign-product rules. Public code or being a programmer does not settle coverage.

children.label: Full current law was not confirmed
children.summary: Several export-rule documents failed to load, so later amendments and exceptions are unchecked. Your own eligibility depends on nationality, employer and item; none was assessed.

children.label: India: institutions get EDA tool access
children.summary: ChipIN gives Indian academic and R&D organisations shared chip-design tool access via nominated contacts. It is institutional, not individual, and live capacity is unverified.

children.label: C2S and C-DAC run India's programme
children.summary: MeitY's C2S programme and C-DAC Bangalore's ChipIN team run tool access and regional support. Learn how access works; these pages are not job offers or contacts.

children.label: Regional support call already closed
children.summary: The regional-support-centre call had a 23 July 2026 deadline, already past. It describes defined support work (installing, licence checkout) but no individual vacancy.

children.label: Micron assembly plant in Gujarat
children.summary: Micron's filing lists Gujarat assembly and test shipments as a separate milestone. It is not a wafer fab and does not show open engineering jobs or remote access.

children.label: Where a developer can contribute
children.summary: Realistic entry is software around the hardware, not device physics. For each route, check what native tools already do before building anything.

children.label: Memory and serving software
children.summary: Work on memory accounting, KV-cache handling, offload and profiling for inference. vLLM already offers much of this, so only real gaps justify custom work.

children.label: Build a memory ledger for one workload
children.summary: Days 1-30: hand-check weights, KV cache and host memory for one setup. Day 90: compare one native config with one change. Worked if it reproduces; stop if native wins.

children.label: KV-cache and quantization trade-offs
children.summary: Learn the KV-cache size formula, quantization side effects, cache eviction and equal-quality testing. Bytes over bandwidth gives a lower bound only.

children.label: Native tools may make custom work moot
children.summary: vLLM already ships KV allocation, cache dtypes, prefix caching and CPU offload. A wrapper around it may add nothing.

children.label: SSD firmware and storage software
children.summary: Micron Bengaluru roles: SSD firmware simulation (2-4 yrs, strong C/C++) and a firmware DevOps role (10+ yrs, CS degree). Both are search-index snapshots, current openings unknown.

children.label: SPDK: open storage software to learn from
children.summary: Public user-space storage libraries (NVMe, NVMe-oF) with contribution links. Good place to learn; it does not mean a mentor or job.

children.label: Cloud DevOps skills transfer, barriers remain
children.summary: Backend and CI/CD skills carry over to firmware DevOps, but the role still asks 10+ years and a degree. Hardware-specific roles need domain depth.

children.label: Non-NVIDIA accelerator software
children.summary: Compilers, operator support and testing for other chips: Google XLA/TPU, AWS Neuron, Huawei Ascend. The tools already automate a lot; independent correctness tests are the entry.

children.label: Triton: public compiler issue tracker
children.summary: Open compiler project with a public issue tracker. A small, reproduced regression is a legitimate contribution; it is not a hiring channel.

children.label: Portability is not drop-in
children.summary: Ascend's PyTorch adapter ties to specific PyTorch, CANN and driver versions, and a familiar frontend still needs operator-by-operator checks. AI can already write some GPU kernels.

children.label: Compare one operator across backends
children.summary: Days 1-30: pin versions, write an independent reference for one operator. Day 90: with approved hardware, test new shapes and document a gap. Stop if native tools pass.

children.label: Chip design (EDA) software
children.summary: Open-source flows like OpenROAD, Verilator and cocotb let a developer touch chip tooling without a fab. Needs C++/Python, HDL and timing concepts.

children.label: AI already edits EDA code
children.summary: A 2026 paper had coding agents improve OpenROAD: up to 10% better timing, up to 19.4% lower power at 1-10% timing cost. Not proof of jobs.

children.label: Run a small FIFO chip-design flow
children.summary: Days 1-90: build a 4-deep FIFO, check 100,000 transactions against an independent model, run OpenROAD on the educational Nangate45 library. Stop if setup passes 8 hours unresolved.

children.label: Educational flow is not real silicon
children.summary: Nangate45 is non-manufacturable, so results show tool skill only, not tapeout or industrial PDK access.

children.label: Photonics and power-electronics software
children.summary: Control, test and fault-injection software for optical and rack power hardware. Real but thin: one TI 48V bench report, NVIDIA 800V roadmap, Q.ANT open photonic SDK.

children.label: Simulator results are not hardware results
children.summary: Q.ANT's SDK has a CPU simulator, but cloud hardware access was still 'coming months'. Software tests cannot replace calibration on real devices.

children.label: Power software still needs commissioning skills
children.summary: An AWS Hyderabad controls role needs 4+ years of critical-environment work and an engineering degree. A software portfolio does not replace that.

children.label: Energy and grid data software
children.summary: Ordinary backend and data work in energy firms is the most reachable path: Kraken, Modo Energy, Hitachi Energy. Domain skills are learned on the job.

children.label: Hitachi Energy Bengaluru software roles
children.summary: DevOps (5-10 yrs) and test automation (5-8 yrs) roles sit inside an energy vendor and need no power-systems degree. Shows mainstream engineering counts here.

children.label: Proxima Fusion needs no fusion background
children.summary: Munich on-site simulation-platform role: Python required, no fusion background asked. Work rights and relocation unconfirmed; fusion power by 2031 is not a base case.

children.label: Incumbents already sell the obvious tools
children.summary: Kraken sells smart scheduling, Siemens sells congestion software and NVIDIA schedules around power limits. A new entrant needs a specific gap.

children.label: Flexible AI data centres
children.summary: A Phoenix test cut a 256-GPU cluster's power 25% for 3 hours, twice, by throttling and pausing jobs. One cluster; strict serving untouched.

children.label: Log power events with decision-time data
children.summary: Days 1-30: build a toy log of events, meter boundary, forecast time and command time; check with independent SQL. Worked if bad cases are blocked; stop if native tools suffice.

children.label: Real savings and reliability unproven
children.summary: Facility-level megawatts, interactive-request deadlines, deferred-work catch-up and arbitrary event timing were not shown. Savings against SLA penalties is open.

children.label: Honest limits of this research
children.summary: What the notes could not settle, so the map is not read as a forecast.

children.label: No 2031 job counts or shortage forecast
children.summary: The notes use small hand-picked samples of roles and vendor claims. They do not forecast hardware vacancies or lasting premiums for human developers.

children.label: Automation may shrink the entry points
children.summary: AI already helps write kernels and EDA code. Smaller teams, cheaper software or new tasks are all possible, so ordinary backend and data work stays a valid path.

children.label: Robotics & physical systems
children.summary: Physical AI is a real but narrow frontier: robots earn money on bounded jobs, humanoids and home robots remain speculative, and accessible software work is operations, evaluation and data. Hardware access, credentials and location are the main barriers.
headlines: Robots are growing fast (5M factory robots, 1M at Amazon) but mostly as single-purpose machines; only ~7,000 humanoids were sold in 2025.
Robot deployments do not guarantee software jobs: service work is heavy, suppliers cut staff, and no one has audited how many roles are software.
The best entry is reliability work around a paid workflow (operations, replay, evaluation, inspection), proven by honest measurement against a simple baseline.
Hardware access, PhD-level research roles and location or work-authorization limits are real barriers that remote-only portfolios cannot fully remove.

children.label: What is real today
children.summary: Robots at scale are mostly specialized machines doing one bounded job. Humanoids and general home robots are far behind.

children.label: Factory and warehouse robots are big
children.summary: Industrial robots and warehouse fleets are already large and growing, though mostly single-purpose machines, not human-shaped workers.

children.label: 5 million factory robots running
children.summary: IFR (Sept 2026): 5M industrial robots operating, 600,000+ installed in 2025 (up 11%). China is 59%; Japan and parts of Europe fell.

children.label: Amazon passed 1 million robots
children.summary: Amazon announced its millionth robot in June 2025 and a fleet-coordination model. Its 10% travel-efficiency gain is a vendor projection.

children.label: Only ~7,000 full-size humanoids sold
children.summary: IFR counts ~250,000 professional service robots sold in 2025 but only ~7,000 humanoids; most humanoid uses are narrow and often teleoperated.

children.label: Field robots win on narrow jobs
children.summary: Farming, mining and inspection robots sell a measurable outcome (less spray, tonnes hauled), not a replacement for the whole worker.

children.label: Mining: ~700 autonomous trucks
children.summary: Caterpillar (Jan 2026): nearly 700 autonomous trucks, 11+ billion tonnes hauled. Construction sites are still a future test market.

children.label: People stay in the loop
children.summary: Rail drones use trained pilots, subsea ROVs are shore-controlled, pipe robots are operated by company staff. Hazard moves away from people; paid human work doesn't vanish.

children.label: Humanoids: narrow work, unproven economics
children.summary: Humanoids now do real but narrow work. The business case rests on utilization assumptions, and research models still fail on new task combinations.

children.label: Agility: 100,000 totes moved
children.summary: Agility reported 100,000+ tote moves at a GXO site. Stronger than a staged clip, but not proof of general labor or a published cost per useful hour.

children.label: Cost swings $16 to $51 per hour
children.summary: Derived from Agility's own $8,500/month price: $16.35/hour at 6,240 working hours, $51/hour at 2,000. Utilization matters as much as price.

children.label: Models fail on unseen task combos
children.summary: RoboCasa365 leader scores 86.5% on seen atomic tasks but 45.2% on unseen composite tasks in simulation; several baselines score 1-3%.

children.label: Robotaxis and drones are real, costly
children.summary: Waymo and Wing run commercial service at scale, but with huge capital, recalls and hidden human-support numbers.

children.label: Waymo: 15 cities, $5B loan, a recall
children.summary: Oct 2026: 15th U.S. city and $5B loan on top of $16B equity. A June 2026 recall covered 3,871 systems entering freeway construction zones.

children.label: Remote-help staffing is not disclosed
children.summary: Waymo says ~70 remote-assistance agents serve ~400,000 weekly trips but withholds how often they step in. Human cost per trip is unknown.

children.label: Robots do not equal software jobs
children.summary: Robot sales do not automatically create accessible software jobs. Much of the work is local service, and suppliers cut staff in downturns.

children.label: Service and support eat margins
children.summary: Selling robots is real revenue, but maintenance, integration and on-site labor are heavy and often handled by others.

children.label: Symbotic services lost money, then improved
children.summary: Symbotic's FY2025 operation-services line had a -6.96% derived gross margin; Q3 FY2026 improved to 11.55%. Walmart is ~85% of revenue.

children.label: Teradyne robotics: ~400 laid off
children.summary: Teradyne's robotics unit lost $99.4M in 2025 and restructured ~400 staff, then recovered to $100M quarterly revenue. Supplier teams are cyclical.

children.label: AutoStore: native tools cover a lot
children.summary: AutoStore reports 72.2% gross margin and ships its own diagnostics and maintenance tools. A generic robot-dashboard startup must beat what is already included.

children.label: Robot adoption does create technical work
children.summary: Operators report more reliability, maintenance and engineering jobs, but nobody has audited how many are software roles.

children.label: Amazon: 30% more technical roles
children.summary: Amazon says its newest fulfillment center type needs 30% more reliability, maintenance and engineering staff. Net jobs and software share are not given.

children.label: Existing open tools already compete
children.summary: Equinor publishes Flotilla, a free robot-fleet operator interface, plus a mock-robot test suite. A new platform needs a clear edge over this.

children.label: What the AI research shows
children.summary: Learned robot policies are improving, but success on benchmarks is narrow and hard to compare. Measuring and recovering from failures is the open gap.

children.label: Benchmark scores and transfer claims are narrow
children.summary: High scores often hide shortcuts: small models match big ones until the scene or goal changes, and shared data transfers only onto known robots.

children.label: Open X-Embodiment: 3x on one skill set
children.summary: RT-2-X got 75.8% vs 27.3% on skills from another robot's data, but on robots already trained. The smaller multi-robot model lost to per-robot RT-1 in all three tables.

children.label: Tiny 0.54M model hits ~95% on LIBERO
children.summary: MINERVA scores ~95% on standard LIBERO with no language understanding, but drops to ~46-56% under camera and lighting changes. Preprint.

children.label: DreamZero: 49% progress, 22.5% full success
children.summary: On unseen tasks it beats other models (12.5% and 7.5% full success) but needs two top-end GPUs and often finishes only part of a task. Preprint.

children.label: Low-attention autonomy is unmeasured
children.summary: RoboArena ranked 7 policies over 612 real-robot comparisons, but never reported how much human setup and watching was needed per finished task.

children.label: Software jobs and routes in
children.summary: Software work sits around the robot: operations, evaluation, perception, firmware, networks and data. Few of these need a PhD, but most need hardware or domain access.

children.label: Robot platform and operations software
children.summary: Versioned robot APIs, telemetry, replay, incident triage, edge runtime. Closest to backend skills; FieldAI's posting asks degree or equivalent, C++/Python, onsite Irvine.

children.label: Policy evaluation and recovery tooling
children.summary: Decide which model version is safe for a bounded task, detect failures, pick data to fix them. Needs ML and statistics; hosted APIs may hide the signals needed.

children.label: Inspection and quality-vision software
children.summary: Make cameras give accepted pass/fail decisions linked to work orders. Competes with mature vendors like HALCON; value is in decision reliability, not a generic model.

children.label: State estimation and perception
children.summary: Robot localization that knows when it is wrong. Needs math (SE(3), filters) and hardware. One sampled role wanted a graduate student; platform work may not.

children.label: Embedded firmware and real-time
children.summary: Interrupts, sensor timing, safe updates in C. Samsara wants 8+ years; Garmin lists an entry-level role. Board-free practice covers only part.

children.label: Telecom and edge network software
children.summary: Cloud-native 5G functions, test automation, network telemetry. Ericsson Bangalore posting: containers, Python/Robot automation, no RF PhD asked. Not a proven shortage.

children.label: Geospatial and satellite data products
children.summary: Turn satellite data into reviewable decisions (crop, flood). Real buyers exist, but nothing here proves rising headcount; wrapper work faces cheap foundation models.

children.label: Field deployment technician
children.summary: Commissioning, repairs, operator training. Real work, but ANYbotics' 'remote' role is US-based with up to 80% travel and hardware skills.

children.label: Barriers: hardware, credentials, place
children.summary: The main blockers are physical access, research credentials and location or work-authorization limits. Remote-only portfolios cannot fully replace field experience.

children.label: PhD roles vs engineering roles
children.summary: Research-scientist jobs want PhDs and publications; platform engineering roles accept equivalent experience. 'Robotics jobs' is too broad a category.

children.label: Hardware and field time are required
children.summary: Timing, calibration, sensor failure and safe stopping are learned on real machines. Simulation and replay cannot validate smoke, water, contact wear or safety.

children.label: Location and work authorization filter roles
children.summary: Sampled postings restrict by place: Deterrence needs U.S. person status, ANYbotics is U.S.-based, Caterpillar's Chennai post needs a degree and has closed.

children.label: Open data often bans commercial use
children.summary: MVTec datasets and the Hilti construction data are non-commercial licenses; some code has no license. Portfolios built on them can't become products directly.

children.label: Skills worth learning
children.summary: The durable combination is software systems plus physical grounding: geometry, timing, and honest measurement of failures.

children.label: Coordinate frames, geometry, estimation
children.summary: Rigid transforms, quaternions, time sync, basic Kalman/factor-graph ideas. Most errors in robot data are frame or clock bugs, not model bugs.

children.label: Latency, clocks and stale data
children.summary: Separate when a sensor saw something, when the system got it, and when an action took effect. Reject expired observations; a fast decision on old data is still wrong.

children.label: Evaluation statistics for robots
children.summary: Hold out whole sessions or sites, count every failed or aborted attempt, report false completions, and beat a simple baseline before claiming a gain.

children.label: Concrete ways in
children.summary: Each starter project is small, uses public data and is built to expose its own failures. Stop it if a simple baseline matches the fancy version.

children.label: Robot data replay and trace tool
children.summary: 30d: wrap an existing estimator on TUM RGB-D data with timestamps and expiry. 90d: add a second sensor. Works if pose error is under 10 cm and replay reproduces failures.

children.label: Localization that admits it's lost
children.summary: 30d: reproduce a baseline on Boreas data. 90d: add a validity signal. Works if undetected error falls 30% on unseen sessions; stop if a simple gate matches.

children.label: Policy failure detector in simulation
children.summary: 30d: reproduce a baseline on LIBERO or RoboCasa. 90d: add a failure detector and recovery. Works if failures drop with under 10% speed loss; stop if a state machine matches.

children.label: Synthetic inspection harness
children.summary: 30d: build synthetic parts with known defects and a classical vision baseline. Works if false rejects are 1% or less and recall 95%+; stop if no buyer owns the decision.

children.label: Firmware timing and safe-update test
children.summary: 30d: spec a sensor pipeline, test against Zephyr's queue. 90d: reproduce MCUboot update tests with interrupted resets. Works if every data loss is visible; stop if upstream covers it.

children.label: Network trace audit in a simulator
children.summary: 30d: map one report-to-command flow in NIST's O-RAN simulator, marking each timestamp. 90d: compare native late-command handling. Works if stale-data cases are flagged; stop if native logs answer it.

children.label: Flood or crop screening from satellite data
children.summary: 30d: use UK Rural Payments Agency ground data, spatial hold-out, cheap spectral baselines. Works if priority recall rises 10 points at a fixed false-alert rate; stop if an index matches.

children.label: Projects and teams to learn from
children.summary: These public projects and groups show real work, tools and entry routes. None is a confirmed job offer.

children.label: Equinor Flotilla and Armada
children.summary: Operator-built multi-robot interface and mock-robot test suite, EPL-2.0. Good for studying real mission, error and security design before writing your own.

children.label: OpenVINS and evo
children.summary: Open VIO estimator and trajectory-evaluation tool, both GPL. Accepting small reproducible fixes is a realistic first contribution; no issues were posted.

children.label: Open Cosmos (satellite software)
children.summary: UK company with edge-computing and ground-platform roles. Hybrid UK, requires right to work there; shows what onboard versus ground work asks.

children.label: Space is a risky first target
children.summary: Orbital demos are mostly numerical feasibility, not live operations: one flood-detection test ran on an uploaded dataset after a power fault. Onboard software needs target hardware.

children.label: Science, security & other sectors
children.summary: Beyond core software, real developer work exists in health data, labs, security, finance and public services, mostly as integration, measurement and reliability. Quantum and creative/consumer bets carry far more risk.
headlines: Across every sector, the reachable work is making AI reliable inside real workflows (data meaning, evaluation, permissions), not inventing the science or the model.
Security (especially post-quantum migration and agent permissions) and finance/payments have the clearest present work; quantum is a deliberate specialist bet with no proven 2031 job market.
Big trial and deployment headlines usually hide narrow results (e.g., no mortality proof, self-reported savings), and platforms or incumbents often absorb generic products.
No source gives hiring or salary forecasts to 2031; pick one domain where you can get a real partner and data, and keep a small side experiment.

children.label: Health, genomics & clinical AI
children.summary: Real deployments and trials exist, but results are narrow. The accessible work is integration, data meaning and measurement, not clinical decisions.

children.label: Breast-screening AI trial is strong evidence
children.summary: About 106,000 women: AI-assisted reading found more cancers (sensitivity 80.5% vs 73.8%) and cut reading workload about 44%.

children.label: But it did not prove fewer deaths
children.summary: Interval-cancer drop (82 vs 93) was not statistically significant; only noninferior. No mortality result, one country, not autonomous diagnosis.

children.label: Scribe AI cuts burnout, savings are modest
children.summary: Randomised trial of 66 clinicians: exhaustion down 0.44 points, note time down 0.36 hours per 8-hour day. Open-label, self-reported, no patient-health outcome.

children.label: Hospital deterioration-alert AI showed no benefit
children.summary: A randomised ward trial of an AI risk display (10,422 visits) found no significant improvement. Not proof of harm, but prediction alone did not help patients.

children.label: Health-data interoperability engineering
children.summary: FHIR and OMOP data work: keep IDs, units, vocabularies and versions meaning the same across systems. Existing validators do much already; value is in the gaps.

children.label: Pin exact versions of FHIR, OMOP, profiles
children.summary: OMOP CDM 5.5.0 (Aug 2026) and FHIR R4/R5 are different contracts; switching versions silently breaks meaning.

children.label: Build a small meaning-checking data test
children.summary: In 30 days, write a synthetic-data reconciliation test between two formats and report every field whose meaning changed. Stop if native validators already catch everything.

children.label: Genomics workflow and benchmarking software
children.summary: Compare variant calls against the right truth set and reference, and report exactly what was measured. Thin pipeline launchers face heavy automation.

children.label: Isomorphic Labs hires engineers, in London
children.summary: Current job board had inference-platform and ML research-engineer roles with no PhD required for the former; all require 3 days a week in London.

children.label: AI drug discovery is still clinical-risk heavy
children.summary: Rentosertib phase III only began dosing in Sept 2026 and is unapproved. Long timelines, big capital and credentials make this a weak default bet for a software engineer.

children.label: Autonomous labs & materials science
children.summary: Robot labs and atomistic AI models work in narrow cases. Best entry for a robotics/ML engineer is the instrument-and-evaluation layer, not inventing new science.

children.label: AI agents ran a real X-ray robot lab
children.summary: A March 2026 study had AI agents operate an X-ray nanoprobe and polymer-film robot, but tasks were narrow (four repeats each) and humans still loaded and calibrated.

children.label: A-Lab's discovery claims were corrected
children.summary: Jan 2026 correction: 'new' meant new to its own platform. 36 of 40 successes were confirmed, 4 inconclusive, one compound removed.

children.label: Atomistic AI models: good tools, easy to misuse
children.summary: MACE and UMA reproduce DFT in many cases, but lower average error does not guarantee stable dynamics or correct physical properties; checkpoint, licence and reference energies matter.

children.label: Instrument control and experiment-ledger engineer
children.summary: Deterministic instrument commands, fault recovery, data lineage and negative-result capture. Transfers to robotics, manufacturing and energy.

children.label: Learn lab data and model-evaluation basics
children.summary: EPICS-style instrument control, leakage-aware splits, calibrated uncertainty, and checking a model against a held-out system.

children.label: Build a simulated lab workflow
children.summary: In 90 days, build one reproducible instrument workflow with constrained commands, simulated faults and a full experiment ledger. Stop if you cannot find a domain scientist to review it.

children.label: Funded but cyclical, credential-gated
children.summary: Lab-software contracts exist (a GBP 202,652 LIMS award) but are often sole-supplier. Lab-instrument demand is uneven and many posts are grant-funded fixed terms.

children.label: Quantum computing (specialist option)
children.summary: Hardware progress is real, but useful quantum advantage is unproven. Treat it as a deliberate specialist retraining, not a hedge for an app developer.

children.label: Error correction is genuinely improving
children.summary: Google reported a distance-7 memory on 101 qubits, with logical error 0.143% per cycle and error shrinking 2.14x per size step.

children.label: Memory fidelity is not a working algorithm
children.summary: Quantinuum's 99.9995% claim is for logical memory only, not long computations. A million steps at similar error rates would rarely all succeed.

children.label: Big roadmaps are targets, not results
children.summary: IBM aims for 200 logical qubits and 100 million gates by 2029; DARPA is still testing whether useful machines are reachable by 2033.

children.label: Entry is classical software inside the quantum stack
children.summary: Compilers, simulation, error-correction decoders, controls and HPC integration. Decoder research roles want research evidence, not just coding.

children.label: Riverlane decoder role is research-heavy
children.summary: Cambridge hybrid role accepts a Master's/PhD or industry equivalent, but also asks for independent theoretical research. Sponsorship unclear.

children.label: Reproduce one error-correction benchmark
children.summary: In 90 days, reproduce one paper's classical baseline with Stim/PyMatching and honest error accounting. Stop if it's only fear of missing out or math prerequisites clash with your goals.

children.label: Security, PQC & confidential AI
children.summary: Security work grows as AI creates more agents, identities and software. Engineers who can prove a system stays within its authority have durable skills, though platforms absorb generic products.

children.label: Old basics still cause most breaches
children.summary: Verizon's 2026 report: exploited vulnerabilities were 31% of breach entry points and third parties were involved in 48%. Vendor-reported data.

children.label: AI agents are easy to hijack
children.summary: A public red-team contest logged 8,648 successful attacks from 67,634 judged submissions across 13 models. It is an upper bound for one attack setup, not real-world frequency.

children.label: Enforce limits outside the model
children.summary: Designs like CaMeL track data provenance and enforce permissions in code rather than trusting the model to refuse. Policy writing and identity context remain hard.

children.label: Post-quantum crypto migration
children.summary: Already a classical integration job: find where cryptography really protects something, check what is negotiated, keep authentication working, and verify rollback.

children.label: Hybrid TLS is now a standard
children.summary: RFC 10024 (Aug 2026) defines X25519MLKEM768 and other hybrids; OpenSSL 3.5 ships ML-KEM natively. Key exchange only, not full certificate migration.

children.label: Build an offline crypto-inventory ledger
children.summary: In 30 days, build a synthetic inventory-to-negotiation-to-rollback test showing which group each connection used. Stop if native OpenSSL tooling already answers it.

children.label: Confidential AI needs layered proof
children.summary: Hardware attestation protects data from infrastructure operators, but does not by itself prove which model ran, who authorised it, or that output is correct. Native verifiers are the baseline.

children.label: AI security engineer, agent identity roles
children.summary: Production AI security, agent platform security and identity for autonomous workloads. Existing security teams may absorb these rather than create new titles.

children.label: Generic agent-security startups look risky
children.summary: Big platforms already sell agent policy, identity and observability. Regulation alone does not give a startup customers or a moat.

children.label: Finance & payments
children.summary: Strongest practical wedge for an application/AI engineer: reliable money data, reconciliation and fraud tooling, where a measurable cost exists.

children.label: Payment volume is huge
children.summary: India's UPI recorded about 24,068 million transactions in Sept 2026; Stripe reported USD 1.9 trillion in 2025 volume, up 34%.

children.label: Volume is not developer income
children.summary: Payment volume is not company revenue or jobs. Stripe's USD 1 billion suite run rate was a projection.

children.label: Ledger, reconciliation and settlement work
children.summary: Keep authorised, posted, paid-out and bank-received states separate; match orders, provider records and bank statements; unmatched amounts stay unmatched.

children.label: Learn money-state and exception handling
children.summary: Explicit currency units, immutable events, reversals instead of edits, bounded one-to-many matching, exception queues.

children.label: Pilot a read-only reconciliation matcher
children.summary: With one finance operator and anonymised data, build matching plus explanations in 90 days. Example gate: 30% less review time at no worse error cost; stop if errors cost more.

children.label: Fraud and dispute tooling
children.summary: Streaming risk features, label timing, dispute evidence assembly. A chargeback is not a perfect fraud label, and high ROC-AUC can still flood reviewers.

children.label: Incumbents and regulation limit new products
children.summary: Matching, dispute drafting and risk scoring already have established providers. Holding funds or underwriting is a regulated, much bigger scope than integrating providers.

children.label: Public sector, legal & education
children.summary: Governments and schools are deploying AI, mostly with narrow measured wins. Reachable work is document handling, case systems and measurement; procurement and trust are the barriers.

children.label: UK government is paying for AI planning tools
children.summary: GBP 8.2m contract (Google Cloud, DeepMind, Faculty) for planning triage; halving decision time is an aim, not a result.

children.label: Platforms and incumbents win procurement
children.summary: UK government stopped its Redbox tool because secure LLM tools came bundled in existing deals. A council kept its existing case system (GBP 208,000) over switching.

children.label: Case and evidence software engineer
children.summary: Turn messy documents into reviewable records, with citations, permissions and error measurement. Deciding legal merits is a separate, qualified role.

children.label: Learn cited retrieval and permission testing
children.summary: Citation correctness, missing-document checks, leakage tests and blind expert review on new cases.

children.label: Prototype an evidence assistant with one expert
children.summary: Pick one bounded process and an expert; measure unsupported claims and review time over 90 days. Stop if provenance or permissions can't be established.

children.label: Open platform DIGIT: real work, hard access
children.summary: eGov's open-source DIGIT powers Odisha's SUJOG; the tender needed large primes (INR 100 crore turnover, 250 staff), so solo entry is hard.

children.label: AI tutoring helps only when designed for learning
children.summary: Plain AI help raised practice scores but cut later unaided exam scores 17%; teacher safeguards removed the harm. Structured tutors and tutor-assist tools showed gains.

children.label: Creative, accessibility & climate
children.summary: Smaller or riskier markets. Value sits in controllable pipelines, task-completing interfaces and decision-linked environmental software, not in demos.

children.label: Games hiring is rough; platform pay is skewed
children.summary: GDC 2026: 28% of 2,300+ respondents reported layoffs, 52% viewed gen-AI negatively. Roblox paid creators USD 1.5bn but median DevEx receipts were about USD 1,500.

children.label: Production-pipeline and tools engineer
children.summary: Make generated and authored assets editable, versioned and reviewable: timing, identity, rights, QA. Attractive generated clips alone are not a portfolio.

children.label: Accessible, task-completing interfaces
children.summary: Voice, screen-reader and vision flows that let a person finish and recover a real task. OS vendors already ship strong voice control, so wrappers are at risk.

children.label: Low word-error is not task success
children.summary: A model can mishear harmless words yet keep the command, or flip a date; ASR was twice as wrong for Black speakers in a 2020 study (0.35 vs 0.19).

children.label: Android XR is real but unproven commercially
children.summary: Developer Preview 4 and glasses libraries exist, yet an SDK is not a profitable app market. Keep skills portable across phone and glasses.

children.label: Water and flood software works beside experts
children.summary: Time-series pipelines, forecast replay and workflow integration for utilities and flood teams. Mature physics tools (EPANET, Flood Modeller) are the baseline to beat.
